messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Thanh is a 46-year-old Vietnamese-American firefighter, divorced, who presented for psychological assessment following a referral from his department's employee assistance program. He served for two years as a volunteer relief worker attached to an international humanitarian organization operating in an active conflict zone in the Middle East, returning to the United States approximately three years ago. His PCL-5 score of 44 places him in the moderate-to-severe range, and the picture that emerged across the intake and first two sessions was one of a man whose interior life has been reorganizing itself, quietly and catastrophically, around what he witnessed and failed to prevent.

During his deployment, Thanh was stationed at a field clinic when a mortar strike hit a civilian shelter adjacent to the compound. He described running toward the structure and finding survivors, including women and children who had been subjected to sexual violence before the attack. The details he encountered in those hours — the particular silence that had preceded the blast, the sounds of the explosion itself, the things people said about what had been done to the women — lodged in him in ways he did not immediately recognize as injury. He worked for eleven more months after that day before being rotated home.

The memories do not come to him as a coherent story. Thanh has said, more than once, that he knows what happened but cannot find the words to explain it — that when he tries to speak, the account breaks apart in his hands. The sequence is wrong; he cannot reliably place events before or after one another. What does arrive with terrible fidelity is the physical dimension: a pressure across his chest and a burning in his forearms that he recognizes, in retrospect, as the sensation of pulling debris away from bodies. When a trigger breaks through — a car backfiring in the station yard, a colleague making a careless comment about sexual violence during a news discussion, or a moment when someone behaves in a way that strikes him as morally contemptible — the memory surges forward not as recollection but as reinstatement, and with it comes the physical pain. These triggers do not merely recall the past; they activate the full appraisal structure he has built around it, and he finds himself flooded immediately with shame and the conviction that he acted in ways that go against who he is. He had made decisions that day — which survivors to reach first, what to prioritize — and he has come to believe those decisions were a form of moral failure that defines him permanently.

That belief — that he is a man whose values collapsed under pressure — has become the organizing principle of his current distress. He is certain that his life has been destroyed by what happened, and he experiences a pervasive sense of belonging nowhere: not among his firefighter colleagues, who he feels cannot understand, and not among his family, from whom he has grown distant since his divorce. These appraisals do not remain static. They feed back into his perceptual world, so that ordinary stimuli become charged with menace — an unusual quiet in the firehouse, the kind of silence that preceded the blast, now reliably produces a sense that something catastrophic is imminent. The shame and the sense of permanent damage amplify his irritability, and he has had two formal complaints filed against him for aggressive outbursts at the station, which has only deepened his conviction that he is fundamentally altered.

To manage the threat he feels almost constantly, Thanh has developed a set of private rituals — sequences of counting and mental repetition that he performs when he senses danger, believing they may prevent another catastrophe. He also works hard to suppress any conscious engagement with the traumatic material, pushing the memories down whenever they surface. But both strategies have compounded his difficulty: the suppression keeps the memories fragmented and wordless, preventing any coherent processing, and the effort of constant vigilance and ritual sustains the physiological arousal that makes the threat feel perpetually real. On nights when the rituals fail and the memories break through fully, he has hurt himself physically — pressing his forearms against the edge of his locker, he said, because the sharp sensation is the only thing that interrupts the loop.

What brought him to seek help was not the outbursts or the self-harm, which he had concealed successfully, but a moment three weeks ago when he froze completely during a residential fire call — stood outside the building in full gear and could not move. He is afraid, he said quietly at the end of the second session, that he has become someone who cannot do the one thing he knows how to do. What he hopes for, though he struggles to believe it is possible, is to find some way back to himself.
